# From findings to modeling decisions {#sec-eda-summary}













A pilot experiment has one job: to tell you what to change before you run the real thing. Nobody grades a pilot by how thorough the notes are. You grade it by whether the next experiment is different because of it. An exploratory analysis is the same kind of object. By now you have a thick notebook on `cell_data`: a design table, a validated cleaning script, one missing value with a story attached, density and raincloud plots, a free session of dragging variables around, and a correlation matrix. A notebook that never turns into "so here is what I will do differently" is wasted bench time, however neat the handwriting (@fig-eda-summary-loaf).

![A pilot loaf is graded by what you change in the next batch. An exploration is the same: it earns its keep when the model you build is different because of it.](images/eda-summary_test-loaf.png){#fig-eda-summary-loaf fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a rustic table with a small, slightly overbaked test loaf on a striped cloth beside an open notebook of scribbles and a pencil, and a wooden cooling rack with four larger, evenly golden loaves on the right."}

This chapter does that translation, once, for everything this part has shown you. It is also where I keep the promise made when we opened the part: "the running list of things we now know about `cell_data` that will shape every modeling decision from here on."

## Four kinds of looking

We did not look at `cell_data` seven times in the same way. We looked in four different ways, and which kind of evidence you are holding decides how far you can lean on it.

**Audit evidence** came first, on purpose. @sec-eda-first-look, @sec-eda-data-quality and @sec-eda-missing-data treated the file as an object before treating it as a dataset: what a row is, which cells are empty, which names are misspelled, which column is another one in disguise. Nothing in that evidence needs a model, and it is the cheapest kind there is. It also set the order of the whole part, because there is no point drawing a figure of numbers you do not yet trust.

**Directed evidence** came next. In @sec-eda-ggplot I chose the question and then chose the geometry that would answer it (a density plot, a scatter, a raincloud), so every conclusion there is only as good as the question I thought to ask. **Generated evidence** is the opposite temperament. @sec-eda-gwalkr asked no question at all; it let you drag variables around and see what jumped out, which is why it ended by handing you a hypothesis to verify rather than a conclusion to report. And **structural evidence**, from @sec-eda-ggpairs, answered a question that no one-pair-at-a-time plot would have answered efficiently: which variables in the whole table are quietly telling the same story twice.

None of the four substitutes for the others (@fig-eda-summary-instruments). The one-click report in @sec-eda-first-look found the missing value and missed the design. The Table 1 described the groups and hid their spread. The raincloud plot showed the spread and could not tell us why a value was missing. That is the practical case for using all of them, in this order.

![Four ways of looking at one dataset: a checkup, a telescope aimed at a chosen target, a kaleidoscope you shake to see what appears, and a board of strings joining everything to everything. None replaces the others.](images/eda-summary_four-ways-of-looking.png){#fig-eda-summary-instruments fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of four objects in a row on a wooden table: a coiled green stethoscope, a brass telescope on a tripod, a kaleidoscope tube with colorful glass fragments spilling from its end, and a small corkboard with five pins joined by loops of teal yarn."}

## The running list

One bookkeeping note before the list, so that no number below looks like a contradiction. The worked example in Part 1 used `Gfap_Intensity`; this part has worked mostly with the integrated density columns `Gfap_IntDen` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`, and with `Tissue_Area`, always the millimeter-squared column and never its micrometer-squared twin (@sec-eda-data-quality explains why). Different columns, not a typo.

@tbl-eda-summary-decisions is the list. Read each row from left to right: what we saw, what it means for a model, and where the book deals with it. Chapters that are still only a title are linked all the same.

| What we saw | What it means for a model | Where the book deals with it |
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **One row is one animal.** 49 rows and 49 unique `MouseID`s (@tbl-eda-intro-design, checked by the `is_uniq` rule of @sec-eda-data-quality). | Independence is a property of the design, not of a plot. Reasonable at this level of aggregation; no longer reasonable if we go back to the per-cell measurements underneath. | @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts, for regions nested in sections nested in animals. |
| **The design is lopsided.** SHAM animals exist only at day 0; MCAO animals run from day 3 to day 30. | Surgery and time cannot be separated for the SHAM comparison, and `Condition * DPI` cannot be estimated. DPI is a progression axis only within MCAO. | @sec-linear-regression-multiple (why the interaction is not estimable) and @sec-count-regression (fold changes against a sham baseline). |
| **Names and units are untidy.** `Tisue_Area` is `Tissue_Area` times 10^6^, and `Pdgfbr_MeanInt` is most likely a misspelled `Pdgfrb_MeanInt`. | Keep `Tissue_Area` (mm²) and never `Tisue_Area`. The raw CSV stays untouched; repairs live in a validated script. | @sec-eda-data-quality; the area becomes the exposure in @sec-count-regression. |
| **One value is missing, and a derived column hid it.** `Pdgfrb_Neg` for animal `Td79`; its `Pdgfrb_Total` counted the gap as zero. | At 1 row in 49, the choice of method barely matters. But any quantity built on `Pdgfrb_Total` (a proportion, for example) inherits a wrong number for that animal. | @sec-eda-missing-data. |
| **Intensities are positive and right-skewed,** and their spread grows with their level. | A Gaussian likelihood is a convenient approximation, not a given. The normality assumption of a linear model concerns the residuals, though, not this raw column. | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions for the residuals; [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) for choosing a family. |
| **The spread changes with time.** The standard deviation of `Gfap_IntDen` is near 25 at day 0 and near 319 at day 7. | Homoscedasticity fails: one `sigma` for every day is too confident at some days and too cautious at others. | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions; the day-3 case left open in @sec-linear-regression-multiple; modeling `sigma` itself in @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression (still to be written). |
| **GFAP at day 30 has two modes.** The mean sits between them and describes neither (@fig-cell_data_rain_EDA). | A single mean, and a single Gaussian, summarize that day badly. The first question is what separates the two groups of animals, which only the lab notebook can answer. | An open question for now; the full time course is revisited in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries (still to be written). |
| **The rise with time is not a straight line** (@fig-cell_data_scatter_EDA). | A linear model is defensible only on a window where the trend is close to linear. | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions (linearity); @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous (the DPI 3 to 14 window). |
| **Some predictors are redundant.** `Pdgfrb_Area` and `Pdgfrb_IntDen`, and `Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen`, each correlate above 0.9 (@sec-eda-ggpairs). | Multicollinearity: putting both members of a pair in one model inflates standard errors and makes the coefficients unstable. | @sec-linear-regression-assumptions (variance inflation factor). |
| **The marker relationship seemed to change with DPI** (@sec-eda-ggplot). | A candidate interaction, but a lead rather than a conclusion. | @sec-linear-regression-multiple fits the one interaction the design allows. |

: From EDA findings to modeling decisions {#tbl-eda-summary-decisions}

A few of those rows deserve more than a line, because the reasoning behind them is more interesting than the table lets on.

**The design row.** It is easy to hear "SHAM exists only at day 0" as a complaint about the experiment, and it is not one. A sham animal went through the surgery without the ischemic event, so it has no lesion and therefore no injury time course to follow. The cost falls on the analysis. The comparison we made in @sec-intro-applied-modeling, sham at day 0 against MCAO at day 3, mixes the effect of the surgery with the passage of time, as the caveat at the opening of this part spells out. The same limit sits quietly inside every fold change in @sec-count-regression, since each one compares a later day with a sham baseline. Nothing in the analysis can repair this. It is a limit on the questions this dataset can answer, and the honest move is to write it next to every result that touches it.

**The last row, on leads and conclusions.** In @sec-eda-ggplot the covariation between the two markers looked different on different days, and I wrote that a model with an interaction would be the natural next step. When @sec-linear-regression-multiple fit the interaction the design does allow (DPI by GFAP, predicting tissue area, so a close cousin of that question rather than the same one), the result was small and uncertain, with a flat line fitting inside every day's interval. That is not EDA failing. It is EDA doing its job: a plot proposes, and a model that reports its uncertainty honestly decides how much weight the proposal deserves. A pattern you can see by eye in 49 animals is a lead. Keep it that way until a model has had a say.

**Two rows no plot of the raw values would have found.** The `Pdgfrb_Total` problem surfaced only because we asked what was *derived from* the column with the hole, and the one-row-per-animal fact only because we asked what a row was and then checked the identifiers. Neither is the output of a function. They are habits of asking, which is the same point @sec-eda-first-look made about one-click report packages: a report puts the same questions to every column, and you get to ask better ones.

**The redundancy row** needs no extra paragraph, because the two chapters involved already split the work cleanly. @sec-eda-ggpairs screened for the redundancy before there was a model; @sec-linear-regression-assumptions quantifies what it does to one.

## EDA as a habit, not a chapter

Here is a debt this part owes. Back in @sec-mcmc-model-checking, the posterior predictive check leaned on the turnkey `pp_check()` because we had not yet learned to build that comparison by hand, and the chapter promised that Part 2 would give us the tools to come back to it. A posterior predictive check is the same move as every figure in this part (put two distributions side by side and look), only the second distribution comes from a model instead of from the bench. So let us reload the informed ischemia model from @sec-priors-regularization, cached and not refit, and rebuild that comparison from `ggplot2` primitives.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(here)
library(brms)

# Same sham (day 0) vs. ischemic (day 3) subset as in Part 1
cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(0, 3))
cell_data_sub$Condition <- factor(cell_data_sub$Condition, levels = c("SHAM", "MCAO"))

# The priors defended earlier
priors_v1 <- c(
  prior(normal(30, 20), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 150), class = "b", coef = "ConditionMCAO"),
  prior(normal(0, 30), class = "sigma")
)

# Reload the informed fit (cached, not refitted)
informed_fit <- brm(
  Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = priors_v1,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/priors-regularization_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)

# 1000 simulated datasets, one per posterior draw (rows) with the same 15 animals (columns)
set.seed(8)
yrep <- posterior_predict(informed_fit, ndraws = 1000)
```
:::






Each row of `yrep` is one complete fake dataset, simulated from one draw of the posterior, with the same fifteen animals as the real one. To compare shapes I draw a hundred of them as faint grey density curves and the real data as one bold curve on top. I push the replicates into the background and give the observed data the single accent color, because the eye should go to the one line that has to be explained and treat the cloud as the yardstick; the orange also differs from the grey in lightness and line width, so the figure still reads in a grayscale printout of the PDF edition (@fig-eda_summary_ppc_rebuild). Each simulated dataset is one `geom_density()` curve, which is why the cloud is made of a hundred thin lines rather than one smoothed band: you can see how much the shape of a fifteen-animal dataset wobbles by chance alone, and judge the real curve against that wobble.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Reshape the first 100 simulated datasets into one long table: a value and a draw id
yrep_df <- data.frame(
  value = as.vector(t(yrep[1:100, ])),
  draw = rep(1:100, each = ncol(yrep))
)

# One faint grey density per simulated dataset, the observed data on top in orange
ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = yrep_df, aes(x = value, group = draw),
    color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_density(
    data = cell_data_sub, aes(x = Gfap_Intensity),
    color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(x = "GFAP intensity", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![A posterior predictive check for the informed ischemia model, rebuilt by hand: 100 simulated datasets (grey) against the observed GFAP intensities (orange).](eda-summary_files/figure-html/fig-eda_summary_ppc_rebuild-1.png){#fig-eda_summary_ppc_rebuild fig-alt='Density plot. One hundred thin grey curves from simulated datasets form a broad cloud with two humps. A thicker orange curve for the observed data lies inside the cloud.' width=576}
:::
:::






It is the same comparison `pp_check(informed_fit, ndraws = 100)` made for us in @sec-mcmc-model-checking, and it tells the same story: the observed curve sits comfortably inside the cloud. The point of rebuilding it is not that the hand-made version is more correct. It is that you can now see every decision `pp_check()` was making on your behalf.

Rebuilding it also lets us do something the turnkey function does not volunteer. The overall shape passes, but this part has already told us something specific to ask: the spread of GFAP is not the same in every group. A posterior predictive check is only as sharp as the statistic you point it at, and EDA is where you learn which statistic to choose. The model we are checking gives sham and ischemic animals one common `sigma`. If the real groups have very different spreads, that model should struggle to reproduce the ratio of the two standard deviations. So for each simulated dataset I compute the standard deviation of the MCAO animals divided by that of the SHAM animals, and compare the whole cloud of ratios with the one we observed (@fig-eda_summary_ppc_sd). A histogram of the simulated ratios with the observed one as a vertical line (`geom_histogram()` plus `geom_vline()`) answers the question in one glance: is the real value somewhere the model could plausibly have produced?






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Which animals are ischemic
is_mcao <- cell_data_sub$Condition == "MCAO"

# SD(MCAO) / SD(SHAM) in each simulated dataset, and in the observed data
sd_ratio_rep <- apply(yrep, 1, function(y) sd(y[is_mcao]) / sd(y[!is_mcao]))
sd_ratio_obs <- sd(cell_data_sub$Gfap_Intensity[is_mcao]) /
  sd(cell_data_sub$Gfap_Intensity[!is_mcao])

# How many simulated datasets reach the observed ratio, and the middle 95% of ratios
n_extreme <- sum(sd_ratio_rep >= sd_ratio_obs)
ci_rep <- quantile(sd_ratio_rep, c(0.025, 0.975))
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Histogram of the simulated ratios with the observed ratio as an orange line
ggplot(data.frame(ratio = sd_ratio_rep), aes(x = ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sd_ratio_obs, color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = sd_ratio_obs, y = Inf, label = "observed",
           color = "#D55E00", hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "SD (MCAO) / SD (SHAM)", y = "Simulated datasets") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Ratio of the standard deviation of MCAO animals to that of SHAM animals, in 1000 simulated datasets (histogram) and in the real data (orange line).](eda-summary_files/figure-html/fig-eda_summary_ppc_sd-1.png){#fig-eda_summary_ppc_sd fig-alt='Histogram of simulated standard deviation ratios, centered near one and spanning roughly zero to four. A vertical orange line for the observed ratio, about 3.4, sits far out in the right tail, beyond almost every bar.' width=576}
:::
:::






The observed ratio is 3.4: the ischemic animals are about 3.4 times more variable than the sham ones. A model with a single `sigma` expects a ratio near 1, and its simulated datasets produce ratios between 0.4 and 2.2 in 95% of cases. Only 5 of the 1000 replicates reach what we actually saw. The density check passed and this one fails, with the same model and the same data, and the only thing that changed was that we knew where to look (@fig-eda-summary-flashlight).

![In the lantern's wide glow the wall looks perfect. A flashlight aimed where exploration told us to look reveals the crack.](images/eda-summary_flashlight-on-the-crack.png){#fig-eda-summary-flashlight fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a plaster wall softly lit by an old lantern on a wooden table at the left, where it looks flawless, while a narrow beam from a flashlight held by a hand entering from the right picks out a thin crack with a few plaster flakes on the floor below."}

::: {.callout-note title="How to report it"}
**Methods.** We checked the fitted model with posterior predictive checks: 100 datasets simulated from the posterior were compared with the observed GFAP distribution, and, because exploration had shown unequal spread, we also compared the ratio of the standard deviations of ischemic to sham animals across 1000 simulated datasets. **Results.** The model reproduced the overall shape of the data, but not the unequal spread: the observed ratio was 3.4, whereas the simulated ratios ranged from 0.4 to 2.2 in 95% of datasets, and 5 of 1000 reached the observed value.
:::

I would not throw out the result of @sec-intro-applied-modeling over this, and I would not wave it away either. The honest move is the one @sec-mcmc-model-checking called "closing the loop": a failed check is the *check* step of the cycle doing its job, and it points at the next *improve* step. Here that means a model that lets the spread differ by group, which is the road from @sec-linear-regression-assumptions (where homoscedasticity becomes a formal assumption) through [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro) (where the family itself is a model for the variance) to the distributional models of @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

A frequentist fit sees the same problem through its residuals. The residuals-versus-fitted plot of @sec-mcmc-model-checking has only two fitted values here, one per group, so it shows two columns of points, and the column for the ischemic animals is far taller than the one for the sham animals. The unequal spread is there whichever way you fit the model. What the Bayesian check adds is the whole distribution of ratios a constant-variance model could produce, so you can say how far outside it the data sit.
:::

The same logic reaches back one more chapter. The five-second glance at plausible GFAP values in @sec-priors-regularization, done "to keep a prior honest", was already EDA, just before it had a name or tools of its own. Once you have the habit of looking before you trust, it stops belonging to any one chapter.

## Opening the door to Part 3

Here is what changes from now on. Everything in this part looked at `cell_data` before a model touched it. Starting with @sec-linear-regression-what, we build a model and ask it to commit to a claim, and the moment a model exists, the informal "I noticed" of this part acquires a formal name and a formal check. Nonlinearity becomes the linearity assumption. The changing spread becomes homoscedasticity. The redundant pairs become multicollinearity, and the lead about the markers becomes an interaction to be estimated, or not. Then the likelihood itself opens up in the generalized models of [the introduction to GLMs](glm-intro.qmd#sec-glm-intro), @sec-logistic-regression, @sec-count-regression and @sec-beta-robust-regression, which is where "positive and right-skewed" stops being a complaint and becomes a design choice.

I will not open that toolkit here. What I want you to carry forward is shorter, and I would pin it above the desk:

::: callout-tip
### The checklist I would keep

1. **Ask what a row is** before anything else (@tbl-eda-intro-design).
2. **Read the table before drawing the plot** (@sec-eda-first-look).
3. **Fix the data in a script, never by hand**, and leave the raw file alone (@sec-eda-data-quality, and the open-science argument of @sec-appendix-open-science).
4. **Ask what depends on every missing value** (@sec-eda-missing-data).
5. **Draw the data by group**, with every point visible (@sec-eda-ggplot).
6. **Screen the whole table for redundancy** (@sec-eda-ggpairs).
7. **Choose the statistic of a posterior predictive check from what EDA showed you** (this chapter).
:::

If you keep to it, nothing in the next part should surprise you. Every crack a regression diagnostic is about to find in `cell_data`, you have already seen first, informally, with your own eyes. That was the order I wanted. @sec-linear-regression-what now stops to ask the plainest question of all: what is that straight line through the points, piece by piece?
